welcome.card: Audiences, messages, flyers, and launch plans for nonprofit clients.
welcome.intro: Marketing is how a small nonprofit gets seen, gets supported, and gets sustainable. PVV's marketing team helps clients with social media, flyers, and promoting their events to Stanford students through the Haas Center. This training walks you through that work with one practice client from start to finish.
welcome.outcome: A one-goal campaign plan, flyer copy, a launch timeline, and a metric you can defend. All of it built for a practice client, ready to adapt for a real one.

modules.title: Your role at PVV

blocks.x: PVV exists to connect local nonprofits and community organizations serving low-income communities with free, student-provided consulting. Marketing is one of three consulting tracks, alongside Financial and Technical.

Under PVV's constitution, marketing help means three things: creating and maintaining a client's online presence (social media), designing and distributing flyers, and promoting client events to Stanford students through the Haas Center for Public Service.

modules.title: One goal, one audience

blocks.x: Small nonprofits rarely struggle with marketing because they're bad at it. They struggle because they try to do everything at once. Your first job is to narrow the plan.

blocks.title: The rule
blocks.x: One goal. One primary audience. One or two channels. Master those before adding anything else.

head: Goal
Measure it by
rows: Followers, reach, or "how did you hear about us" answers

blocks.x: Two audiences, two messages

Most PVV campaigns speak to two groups. The first is the community the nonprofit serves, who find events on Instagram, Facebook, and flyers at laundromats and churches. The second is Stanford students who might attend or volunteer, who hear about things through Haas Center emails and Instagram. They need different words in different places.

modules.title: Message and story

blocks.x: People act when they understand what's happening and why it matters to someone. A key message gives every post, flyer, and email the same spine, so you aren't reinventing the pitch each time.

blocks.title: Key message formula
blocks.x: [Organization] helps [who] by [how]. Right now, we need [specific ask] so that [impact].

Example: Eastside Community Pantry helps low-income families in East Palo Alto by providing free weekly groceries. Right now, we need you at our Taco Tuesday fundraiser on March 15 so that we can keep our shelves stocked through summer.
The caption formula

head: Part
What it does
rows: A question, a number, or a bold statement that stops the scroll
Two or three sentences on why this matters to a real person
Date, time, location, and where to find more
One clear next step, such as "Link in bio to RSVP"

blocks.title: Stories need permission
blocks.x: Before you share a client's photo, name, or story, get their permission and the nonprofit's approval. When in doubt, tell the story without identifying details.

blocks.q: Which caption opening makes the strongest hook?
options: Hello everyone! We are having an event.
Please like and share this post.
200 families eat from our pantry every week. Help us keep the shelves full on March 15.
blocks.explain: A specific number and a stake beat a generic greeting.
blocks.hint: Which one gives a reader a reason to keep reading?

blocks.q: You'd like to feature a photo of a family picking up groceries. What first?
options: Post it. The pantry is public.
Get permission from the family and approval from the nonprofit.
Blur the name and post it.
blocks.explain: Permission comes first, and the client approves what goes out.

modules.title: Design a flyer people read

blocks.x: A stranger at a laundromat bulletin board gives your flyer about three seconds. In that time they should know what's happening, when, where, and what to do next. If any of those is missing, the flyer fails.

blocks.caption: Build the flyer from biggest to smallest. If everything is the same size, nothing stands out.
legend: Event name: biggest, readable from 10 feet
Location: always include the street address
One line on why it matters
QR code and logo: smallest, but always there

blocks.title: The squint test
blocks.x: Zoom out until the flyer is thumbnail-sized. Can you still read the event name and the date? If not, simplify.

Readable also means high contrast. WCAG, the standard for accessible design, asks for at least 4.5:1 contrast between normal-size text and its background, and 3:1 for large text. A free checker will tell you the ratio for any pair of colors.

blocks.title: Canva Design School: Canva Pro for Nonprofits
blocks.why: Watch the lessons on nonprofit templates and Brand Kit. Canva's nonprofit program is free for registered nonprofits, so your clients may qualify. PVV, as a student group, does not.

blocks.title: WebAIM contrast checker
blocks.why: Enter your text and background colors as hex codes and read the ratio.

blocks.title: Write the flyer copy
blocks.intro: Practice client: Eastside Community Pantry, Taco Tuesday fundraiser, March 15, 5 to 8 PM. Colors: forest green and gold.

fields.label: One line on why it matters
fields.placeholder: e.g., Every plate keeps a family's shelves stocked

fields.label: Date, time, and location (make up a realistic address)
Your text and background colors, and the contrast ratio the checker reports

blocks.q: Which element should be the largest text on the flyer?
blocks.explain: The event name comes first in the reading order, then date and time.

blocks.q: The checker says your normal-size text has a 3.1:1 contrast ratio. Does it meet the WCAG AA minimum?
options: No. Normal text needs at least 4.5:1, so darken the text or lighten the background.
blocks.explain: 3:1 is only enough for large text.

checklist: I wrote flyer copy in biggest-to-smallest order
I checked a color pair with the contrast checker

modules.title: Measure and hand off

blocks.x: Posting is half the job. The other half is knowing whether it worked and leaving the client able to carry on without you.

head: Track this
Ignore this, for now
rows: "How did you hear about us?" answers

blocks.x: The Assigned Liaison

Each Bridge Kit has one PVV member as its Assigned Liaison for the quarter. The client approves copy once at kickoff, and the liaison handles posting, recruiting Stanford peers, and attending one client event. At the end of the quarter, the liaison writes a handoff note so the next person can pick up cleanly. The client keeps the logins.

blocks.title: Create your first form in Google Forms
blocks.why: A short form with a "how did you hear about us?" question is the simplest way to measure what worked.

blocks.title: Capstone: your campaign in one place
blocks.intro: Pull your work from this training into one Google Doc or Canva design: goal, audiences, key message, flyer, launch plan, and metric. Set sharing to Anyone with the link can view, then paste the link. Your category chair will review it.

fields.label: What is one thing you would do differently on a real client campaign?

blocks.q: A client's Instagram gained 200 followers but zero new volunteers signed up. What happened?
options: They tracked the wrong metric. Followers aren't volunteers.
blocks.explain: Measure the action you want, not the vanity number.

blocks.q: After the handoff, who holds the client's social media logins?
options: The PVV liaison, so they can keep posting
blocks.explain: The client owns their accounts. PVV never keeps the keys.
